title: Children's rights
hook: a good name, education, fairness between them

segments.voice: Yesterday, talaq, and your line: permitted, not loved. A door the law leaves open, with waiting and kindness built around it. Where did you see something ended gently, or wish it had been? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

The boy in this story is the one who told it. Nu'man ibn Bashir remembered his father walking him to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. His father had given him a gift, and wanted the Prophet to stand witness to it. A simple errand. The Prophet asked the father one question: had he given the same to each of his children? He said no. And the Prophet would not witness it. Nu'man remembered his father turning around and taking the gift back. Today is about what children are owed in Islamic law, and why fairness sits at the center of it.
screen: `A FATHER WANTS A WITNESS.` → `ONE QUESTION: THE SAME FOR EACH?` → `THE GIFT GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: The fiqh books talk about the rights of a child the way they talk about the rights of a spouse: things owed, not favors. Today, three of them. First, a good name. The reports in Sahih Muslim tell of the Prophet changing names he found harsh or heavy into gentler ones. A name is said over and over across a life, by teachers and friends and, one day, on a grave. So choosing it well is counted among a parent's duties. Second, education. In a report in Ibn Majah, seeking knowledge is called a duty on every Muslim, and jurists teach that a parent owes a child the teaching that makes that duty possible: how to read, how to pray, how to live with people, and a way to earn a living. Third, fairness, and here is Nu'man's story again. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells his father to fear God and be just between his children. Not identical in every detail, since children need different things, but no child made to feel like the favorite's shadow. The jurists argue over the edges. Some hold that gifts between sons and daughters should be exactly equal; others follow the shares of inheritance. Both sides start from the same story, where favoritism between children is treated as a wrong, not a private taste. And underneath all three sits the Qur'an itself. It forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, and promises that God provides for them and for their parents. Before a name or a lesson, then, comes life itself.
screen: `RIGHTS OWED, NOT FAVORS.` · `FIRST, A GOOD NAME.` · `THEN, AN EDUCATION.` · `FAIRNESS: FEAR GOD, BE JUST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the children in your life. Your own, if you have them, or nieces and nephews, students, the kids on your street. Picture them in a row. Notice if one face comes easier than the others, the easy one, the funny one, the one who looks like you. No guilt; just notice. Now go down the row slowly and give each one a moment of real attention. Their name. One thing they need right now that is theirs alone. If you pray, you can hold each name in turn. The bell holds the time.
Children's rights. In Islamic law, what a child is owed: life, a good name, an education, and fairness between them and their brothers and sisters. Today's word.

Your line: fair to each. Today, when you give time, praise or a treat to one child, look around for the others. Tomorrow, what a family is owed when someone dies. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Islamic law counts choosing a good name and teaching a child to read, pray and earn a living among a parent's duties; scholars teach that gifts between children should be fair, following the story of Nu'man ibn Bashir.

fork.setup: you're Bashir. you've given one son a gift and walked him to the Prophet to witness it. he asks if all your children got the same. they didn't. what happens?
options: the Prophet tells you to fear God and be just, and you take the gift back.
the Prophet tells you to give it to the eldest instead.
fork.reveal: the Prophet would not witness it, told him to be just between his children, and the father took the gift back.

trapdoor: what you thought: children's rights are a modern idea.
what it means: the fiqh books list what a child is owed: life, a good name, an education and fairness.
what a scholar hears: Nu'man ibn Bashir's report in Bukhari and Muslim, and the jurists' debate on equal gifts versus inheritance shares.

notes: Bukhari 2587 / Muslim 1623: confirm numbers and paraphrase (the gift, the Prophet's refusal to witness, 'fear God and be just between your children', the father taking it back). Some versions name the gift as a servant; confirm.
Muslim 2139: changing names (e.g. 'Asiyah to Jamilah); confirm citation.
Ibn Majah 224: chain discussed by scholars; confirm it is fair to cite as 'a report in Ibn Majah'.
Equal gifts: Hanbali view follows inheritance shares (2:1 male/female), others (majority?) equal; phrased without counts. Confirm framing.
Rights of a child as framed in fiqh (life, name, education, fairness) are a summary; confirm fair.
